title: Nicaea II, 787
hookLine: images are venerated, not worshiped; the honor passes to the one shown

cards: An old photograph, soft at the corners, of a grandmother who has died. Her grandson takes it out of a drawer before a long trip, looks at it a moment, and kisses it. Then he puts it back.

No one watching would say he kissed paper. The kiss went to her. Hold that small, ordinary gesture, because a council of bishops built a careful distinction on almost exactly that: two kinds of honor.
Today's word names one of them: veneration.

teach.b: Earlier this year, this path met John of Damascus, who defended icons when emperors were tearing them down. The argument went on, and the bishops met again at Nicaea.

The Catechism says the seventh ecumenical council, at Nicaea in 787, justified the veneration of icons, of Christ, of the Mother of God, of the angels and all the saints, on the basis of the mystery of the Word made flesh.
Here's the line it drew. Worship, adoration, belongs to God alone. Veneration is respect and honor: a bow, a kiss, a candle.

Catholics give an icon or a statue veneration, never worship. The Catechism quotes Saint Basil to explain why it isn't idolatry: the honor rendered to an image passes to its prototype, to the one it shows.
And the council itself adds: whoever venerates an image venerates the person portrayed in it. Like the kiss on the photograph, it doesn't stop at the paper. It passes through.
Why does the Incarnation matter here? Because the council rested its case on it. John's Gospel says, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
John of Damascus had started his defense there; the council made that starting point the whole Church's.

teach.h: WORSHIP FOR GOD; HONOR FOR IMAGES.
teach.b: So much hangs on one distinction, between worship and honor.
Lose it, and either the icons go, or God gets crowded out.

teach.h: THE HONOR PASSES TO THE ONE SHOWN.
teach.b: Keep it, and the honor passes through.

how: Catholics venerate images by bowing, kneeling, lighting candles or kissing a crucifix or icon, as on Good Friday when the faithful come forward to venerate the cross; the Church teaches that adoration is given to God alone.

games.q: you're at Nicaea. some say any image of Christ is idolatry; others want images back. what line do you draw?
o: ban all images, to be safe.
venerate images, worship God alone; the honor passes to the one shown.
worship the images too; they're holy.
games.why: the council justified the veneration of icons and kept worship for God alone, because the honor passes to the one the image shows.

practice: Bring close an icon, a crucifix, a holy card, or a photograph of someone you love, and look at it for a while, noticing your attention go past the wood and paint to the one it shows.
If it fits you, bow your head to it or kiss it, the way people kiss icons in church. If you pray, let the gesture be your prayer, without words; if you don't, let it simply be thanks.

wordCard.voice: Veneration. Honor given to an image or a saint, never the worship that belongs to God; the honor passes to the one shown. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: bowing down in honor, the word for the veneration given to icons; worship due to God alone is latreia.

carryVoice: Your line: honor passes through. A kiss on paper that reaches a person. That's day seven hundred seventy-five.
